moduleTitle: Individual free will and responses to suffering; knowledge and ignorance

note.specFocus: Individual free will and responses to suffering; knowledge and ignorance.
note.summary:
INDIVIDUAL FREE WILL
Hindus believe that each atman has free will – the ability to choose how to act. The law of karma only makes sense if people are responsible for their choices. Past karma shapes the situation a person is born into (prarabdha karma), but within that situation they are free to choose good or bad actions, which create new karma (kriyamana). A common image is a game of cards: the hand you are dealt is your past karma, but how you play it is your free will.
The Bhagavad Gita stresses personal responsibility: "Let a person lift themselves up by the self; let them not degrade themselves. The self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self" (6.5). At the end of his teaching Krishna tells Arjuna, "Reflect on this fully, then do as you wish" (18.63) – God does not force anyone.
There are debates. Some Hindus stress that the gunas and the senses strongly push a person (Gita 3.27, 3.33), so freedom has to be developed through self-control. Some theistic Hindus believe God, within the heart, guides and ultimately controls all things, while still giving souls freedom to turn towards him or away.

RESPONSES TO SUFFERING
Hindus offer several explanations of and responses to suffering (dukkha):
• Karma – much suffering is the result of a person's own past actions, so it is not random or unjust.
• Ignorance and attachment – suffering comes from identifying with the temporary body and desiring temporary things (Gita 2.62–63: from dwelling on sense objects comes attachment, then desire, anger, delusion and ruin).
• Suffering as a teacher – hardship can produce humility, compassion and a desire for God. Kunti, in the Bhagavata Purana (1.8.25), prays for difficulties so that she will always remember Krishna.
• Equanimity – the Gita teaches tolerating pleasure and pain like the passing seasons (2.14) and remaining the same "in happiness and distress".
• Practical compassion – suffering in others calls for action: seva (selfless service), charity and ahimsa. Gandhi's work for the poor shows this.
Hindus therefore respond with acceptance, prayer and puja, fasting or pilgrimage, and with service to those who suffer.

KNOWLEDGE AND IGNORANCE
Avidya (ignorance) is seen as the root cause of samsara and suffering. It is not lack of information but misunderstanding who we are – thinking "I am the body" instead of recognising the eternal atman. Maya fuels this ignorance.
Vidya or jnana (knowledge) is spiritual wisdom that removes ignorance "as the sun dispels darkness" (Gita 5.16). "There is no purifier in this world like knowledge" (Gita 4.38). The famous prayer of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (1.3.28) asks: "Lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to immortality."
• Advaitins see knowledge (realising atman = Brahman) as the direct means of moksha.
• Vaishnavas see true knowledge as knowing oneself as a servant of God, which naturally leads to devotion.
Knowledge is gained from scripture (shruti and smriti), a qualified guru and personal practice such as meditation.

TODAY
These beliefs encourage British Hindus to take responsibility for their choices, to respond to suffering with resilience and service (e.g. Sewa Day volunteering), and to study scripture in temple classes or at home.

questions.question:
Which one of the following is the Hindu term for spiritual ignorance?
A) Avidya
B) Jnana
C) Dharma
D) Ahimsa
questions.modelAnswer:
A) Avidya.
Avidya is spiritual ignorance – misunderstanding the true self. Jnana is knowledge, dharma is duty, ahimsa is non-violence.

questions.question:
Which one of the following best describes Hindu belief about free will?
A) Everything is fixed by fate
B) People can choose their actions and create new karma
C) Only priests have free will
D) Free will ends at the age of sixteen
questions.modelAnswer:
B) People can choose their actions and create new karma.
Past karma shapes circumstances, but Hindus believe each person is free to choose how to act now (Gita 6.5).
questions.examTip: Karma is not fate – this is a common misunderstanding.

questions.question: Give one Hindu explanation for why people suffer.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: past karma; ignorance (avidya) of the true self; attachment/desire for temporary things; suffering is a test or teacher; the effects of living in Kali Yuga; the actions of others using free will.

questions.question: Give one way in which Hindus believe spiritual knowledge can be gained.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: studying scripture such as the Upanishads or Bhagavad Gita; learning from a guru; meditation; jnana yoga; listening to discourses (satsang) and asking questions.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which Hindu beliefs about suffering influence Hindus today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Many Hindus respond to their own suffering with acceptance and patience, believing it may result from past karma. Following the Gita's teaching to tolerate pleasure and pain like passing seasons (2.14), they try to stay calm and not blame God, often turning to prayer, puja or the recitation of scripture for strength.

Second way: Hindus believe they should help relieve the suffering of others. Because the divine is in all beings, serving people is serving God, so many British Hindus take part in seva – for example volunteering on Sewa Day, giving food at temples, or supporting charities such as Sewa International which provides disaster relief.
questions.examTip: Balance an 'inner' response (attitude) and an 'outer' response (action) to give two distinct ways.

questions.question: Explain two contrasting Hindu views about the relationship between free will and God.
questions.modelAnswer:
First view: Many Hindus emphasise that God does not interfere with free will. Each atman is responsible for its choices and creates its own karma; God, as Paramatma in the heart, only witnesses and advises. Krishna gives Arjuna his teaching and then says 'Do as you wish' (Gita 18.63), showing that people must choose for themselves.

Second view: Other Hindus, especially in some bhakti traditions, stress that everything ultimately depends on God, who directs all beings 'as if mounted on a machine' (Gita 18.61) and grants liberation by his grace. For them, human free will is real but limited; the most important free choice is to surrender to God, who then takes responsibility for the devotee (Gita 18.66).
questions.examTip: Two views from different Hindu emphases count as 'contrasting'.

questions.question:
Explain two Hindu teachings about knowledge and ignorance.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Hindu belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: Ignorance (avidya) is the root cause of samsara and suffering. It means wrongly identifying with the body and mind instead of the eternal atman. The Gita (2.62–63) explains that dwelling on sense objects leads to attachment, desire, anger and delusion, and finally to ruin. Because people do not know who they really are, they chase temporary pleasures and create karma that keeps them in the cycle of rebirth.

Second teaching: Spiritual knowledge (jnana or vidya) removes ignorance and leads towards moksha. Krishna says, 'There is no purifier in this world like knowledge' (Gita 4.38), and that knowledge destroys ignorance as the sun lights up everything (5.16). The prayer of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (1.3.28) asks, 'Lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to immortality.' Hindus gain such knowledge by studying scripture under a guru (Gita 4.34) and through meditation.
questions.examTip: 'Asato ma sad gamaya' is a short, memorable source – useful for several topics.

questions.question:
Explain two Hindu teachings about free will.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Hindu belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: Each person is responsible for their own spiritual progress. The Bhagavad Gita (6.5) teaches, 'Let a person lift themselves up by the self; let them not degrade themselves. The self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is its enemy.' This means humans cannot blame others or God for their choices; by controlling the mind and senses they can rise spiritually.

Second teaching: Free will works within the law of karma. Past karma (prarabdha) shapes the circumstances into which a person is born, such as their family and health, but they freely choose how to act now, creating new karma (kriyamana). The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (4.4.5) says 'As one acts, so one becomes', showing that the future is shaped by present choices. This is why Hindus reject the idea that karma is simply fate.
questions.examTip: Explain the difference between past karma (circumstances) and present karma (choices) to show depth.

questions.question:
'Suffering is always the result of a person's own karma.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Hindu teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS SUPPORTING THE STATEMENT

Many Hindus would argue that the law of karma applies to all experiences. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad teaches, "As one acts, so one becomes" (4.4.5). If this law is universal, then every experience of pain or pleasure is ultimately a result of a person's own past actions, whether in this life or a previous one. Suffering that seems undeserved, such as a child born with an illness, can be explained by prarabdha karma – past karma ripening now.

This view also protects belief in a just universe and a good God. God does not cause suffering; each atman reaps what it has sown. Many Hindus find this a helpful response because it encourages them to accept hardships patiently and to focus on doing good so that their future is better.

ARGUMENTS SUPPORTING A DIFFERENT VIEW

However, other Hindu teachings suggest that suffering also has other causes. Ignorance (avidya) and attachment are themselves said to be the root of suffering: the Gita (2.62–63) describes how desire leads to anger and delusion. Suffering can come from our wrong attitude to events, not just the events themselves – the same loss may cause despair to one person and acceptance to another.

People also suffer because of other people's free choices. If someone is harmed by a criminal or by injustice, it seems more accurate to say that the wrongdoer is responsible. Many Hindus argue that saying victims "deserve" it is a misuse of karma, and it has been criticised for justifying caste discrimination and poverty.

Some suffering can be understood as a test or a spiritual opportunity. In the Bhagavata Purana, Queen Kunti even prays for difficulties because they make her remember Krishna (1.8.25). In this view, suffering is allowed by God for a person's growth, not simply as a reaction to past deeds. Living in Kali Yuga, an age of decline, is also said to bring suffering to everyone.

CONCLUSION

Karma is a central Hindu explanation for suffering, and it is accepted by most Hindus as part of the picture. But the word "always" makes the statement too strong. Hindu teaching also points to ignorance, the free will of others, the conditions of Kali Yuga and suffering as a means of spiritual growth. I therefore conclude that suffering is often, but not always, best explained by a person's own karma, and that whatever its cause, Hindus have a duty to relieve it.
questions.examTip: Words like 'always' invite you to argue for 'sometimes' – use them in your conclusion.

questions.question:
'Ignorance, not wrongdoing, is the main problem for human beings.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Hindu teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS SUPPORTING THE STATEMENT

Many Hindu teachings put ignorance (avidya) at the root of the human problem. Humans suffer and remain in samsara because they misunderstand who they are, identifying with the temporary body and mind rather than the eternal atman. Wrongdoing comes from this mistake: because we think we are the body, we desire possessions and pleasures, become angry when we do not get them, and harm others (Gita 2.62–63). Remove the ignorance and the wrongdoing disappears.

This is especially true in Advaita Vedanta, where liberation comes through knowledge alone: realising "Tat tvam asi" – "You are that" (Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7). Shankara taught that no amount of good action can bring moksha, because action belongs to the world of maya; only knowledge removes ignorance. The Gita agrees that "there is no purifier like knowledge" (4.38) and that the fire of knowledge burns all karma to ashes (4.37).

The great Upanishadic prayer "Lead me from darkness to light" (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.28) also shows that the main spiritual task is to move from ignorance to understanding.

ARGUMENTS SUPPORTING A DIFFERENT VIEW

Others argue that wrongdoing (adharma) is just as serious. The law of karma means that harmful actions themselves bind the soul and cause suffering for others. Someone may know perfectly well that something is wrong and still choose to do it because of greed or anger. Arjuna himself asks, "What makes a person do wrong, even against their will?" and Krishna answers that it is desire and anger (Gita 3.36–37), which suggests that the problem is also moral weakness, not just lack of knowledge.

Many Hindus focus on dharma – right action – as the foundation of life. The avatars descend "when dharma declines" (Gita 4.7), which suggests that wrongdoing in the world is a central problem God himself responds to. In bhakti traditions, the main problem is forgetting and turning away from God; the solution is love and surrender, not just intellectual knowledge.

CONCLUSION

Hindu teaching suggests that ignorance and wrongdoing are closely linked: ignorance of the true self leads to selfish desire, which leads to wrongdoing, which creates karma and further ignorance. I think the statement is largely correct, because most Hindu schools see avidya as the root cause; however, wrongdoing is not secondary, as it causes real harm to others and must be overcome through dharma and devotion as well as knowledge. The best answer is that ignorance is the root, but wrongdoing is the fruit, and both must be addressed.
questions.examTip: Use a 'chain' (ignorance → desire → wrongdoing → karma) – AQA rewards logical chains of reasoning.
